title: Climate-set root-zone storage growth predicts 16% of the lost south-east Australian runoff after 2009 and false losses in northern Australia (174 + 62 catchments, GR4J)
abstract: Question: after 1997, south-east Australian (SE-AU) runoff fell about 20-25% below its 1951-1996 rainfall-runoff relation and stayed low. Does a root-zone storage capacity that vegetation sizes to the largest past drought deficit (a 'ratchet') predict this loss from climate alone? Approach: CAMELS-AUS v2.03 daily data, 174 SE-AU, 62 North-AU (control) and 25 SW-WA catchments. GR4J was calibrated on 1956-1996 only. The production-store capacity X1 followed the mass-curve deficit maximum of the previous 20 years (ratchet) or 3 years (reversible), with no extra free parameter. Results (AGCD rain, 2010-end): the observed mean change was -24.0% (-55.7 mm/yr). The ratchet predicted -11.6% as a mean of catchment ratios (fraction 0.48, 95% CI 0.38-0.60), but only -8.8 mm/yr by volume (fraction 0.16, 0.10-0.23). Almost all of the predicted loss was in dry catchments. In the wet third, which lost 88 mm/yr, it predicted 0.9 mm/yr. It predicted -8.1% in North-AU, where flow rose by 11%, so the pre-set false-positive control failed. It explained 10% (-15 to +35%) of the SE-AU minus North-AU contrast. The reversible model did slightly better than the ratchet. A free capacity elasticity fitted on 1956-1996 had median 0. The flow needs an X1 increase of about x1.5 in all wetness classes, but this does not follow the climatic capacity ratio (Spearman -0.13). Conclusion: a climate-set root-zone ratchet does not explain the persistent loss. Limitations: one model structure, an assumed X1-Sr link, fixed evaporation fraction in the deficit, optimiser noise, a volume-weighted measure added after inspection.
